name: Jumping / basketball / swimming for height

lead: Height-focused communities recommend jumping, basketball and swimming during puberty, saying these sports load the growth plates or stretch and decompress the spine. The idea gets support from the number of tall basketball and water polo players.

Believers describe mechanical loading of bones and spinal decompression as the mechanisms. Reference sources emphasise genetics (60 to 80 percent heritable) and childhood nutrition as the main drivers of height, and no published trial has tested these sports for height gain; athlete studies mostly reflect selection of already-tall players.

paras: People play the sports regularly through the teenage years, often as general activity alongside sleep and nutrition habits, and add jumping drills or swim sessions for the stretching element.
The sports carry ordinary sports-injury risks. No height-specific harms are documented.

chain: Jumping and swimming load or stretch the body
angle.text: Basketball, jumping and swimming are used in adolescence in the belief that they stimulate growth plates and decompress the spine. The belief is helped by how many tall athletes play these sports; no trial has tested them for height gain.

lead: Jumping, basketball and swimming are sports that some looksmaxxing and height-focused communities say can stimulate the growth plates or decompress the spine and so add height during adolescence. The belief is also popular in general fitness lore, partly because many elite basketball and water polo players are tall.

Reference sources describe adult height as 60 to 80 percent heritable, with childhood nutrition and health as the main environmental influences; exercise is mentioned only as one of several external factors.[1] A study of male water polo players found that body build and swimming tests at age 17-18 predicted later career success, which concerns selection of tall athletes rather than sport causing height.[2]
No published trial was found that tests whether these sports increase final height in healthy adolescents.

paras: Proponents recommend regular jumping exercises, basketball and swimming during puberty, often alongside sleep and nutrition advice. Swimming is credited with stretching and decompressing the spine; jumping and basketball are credited with mechanically stimulating long-bone growth.

Elite basketball and water polo squads contain many tall players, which supporters sometimes cite. Researchers studying water polo have measured anthropometric indices as predictors of success among already-selected top-level players, which reflects who is chosen for the sport.[2] Reference works describe height as strongly genetic and note that growth in males typically ends around 18 to 19.[1]
No studies found. A prospective study of male water polo players examined whether swimming capacity and body build predicted long-term career success, not whether the sport increased height.[2]

lore.intro: Height forums commonly list jumping sports and swimming among natural measures to maximise growth in the teen years.

claims.claim: Basketball, jumping and swimming stimulate the growth plates
Swimming decompresses the spine and adds height
